text:
Sampled HR@10 does not reliably establish full-catalog ranking quality. Krichene and Rendle show sampled metrics can reverse model comparisons even in expectation; small candidate sets increasingly behave like AUC. [RecSys 2025 research](https://doi.org/10.1145/3705328.3748086) evaluates sampling reliability through resolution, fidelity, robustness and recovery of model rankings. Thus, weak Electronics separation on diagnostic candidates alone cannot establish poor full-catalog recommendations. [On Sampled Metrics](https://research.google/pubs/on-sampled-metrics-for-item-recommendation/)

Negative selection changes what a diagnostic measures. A [2024 sequential-recommendation study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.17276) finds aggregate accuracy can conceal head/mid/tail disparities: random-negative training favored head items, while popularity-based alternatives sometimes improved balance at an overall accuracy cost. These are training findings, not evidence that popularity-sampled evaluation estimates full-catalog performance. Hard negatives measure a deliberately difficult slice; their results need separate interpretation from uniform-candidate results.

Practical inference: audit the same frozen NextItNet checkpoint on fixed users and targets, using nested uniform candidate sizes, popularity-stratified candidates, and checkpoint-mined hard negatives; compute exact full-catalog ranks for a bounded user subset. Report target rank percentile and uniform pairwise win rate alongside HR@10; percentile normalizes catalog size but does not guarantee invariant outcomes across candidate distributions. Quantify sensitivity through paired user-level differences, bootstrap intervals and top-10 overlap, keeping all candidate draws paired across conditions. Resample users within category before computing macro differences. Separate user uncertainty from variation across negative draws. Keep these audits distinct from the pinned host evaluator; unlabeled recommendation overlap measures stability, not relevance.
